questions.q: Asked whether it is lawful to call one’s country “motherland,” how did the author answer?
options: Only scholars may use the word
Not quite. The article says: It is a matter of culture and sentiment, not of religious law; love of one’s homeland is natural.
It is a religious duty
Not quite. The article says: It is a matter of culture and sentiment, not of religious law; love of one’s homeland is natural.
It is forbidden
Not quite. The article says: It is a matter of culture and sentiment, not of religious law; love of one’s homeland is natural.
It is a matter of culture and sentiment, not of religious law; love of one’s homeland is natural
Yes. Making it a legal question is a form of extremism.
questions.rationale: “It must be regarded as an issue of culture and not of the law… Love for one’s nation, or patriotism is a natural fact.”

questions.q: The Prophet once answered a questioner, “Seek the fatwa from your heart.” What does the editorial take this to mean?
options: The heart is wiser than revelation
Not quite. The article says: Matters not addressed in the Quran and Hadith are to be settled by one’s own sincere conscience.
Matters not addressed in the Quran and Hadith are to be settled by one’s own sincere conscience
Right. With a pure intention.
Questions should not be asked
Not quite. The article says: Matters not addressed in the Quran and Hadith are to be settled by one’s own sincere conscience.
Scholars’ opinions are never needed
Not quite. The article says: Matters not addressed in the Quran and Hadith are to be settled by one’s own sincere conscience.
questions.rationale: “Matters not mentioned directly in the Quran and Hadith should be decided through the dictates of one’s own nature or conscience.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, does happiness always seem to lie in the future?
options: The past was happier than the present
Not quite. The article says: Man seeks perfection but lives in an imperfect world; complete happiness belongs to Paradise.
People do not work hard enough
Not quite. The article says: Man seeks perfection but lives in an imperfect world; complete happiness belongs to Paradise.
Happiness is only an idea
Not quite. The article says: Man seeks perfection but lives in an imperfect world; complete happiness belongs to Paradise.
Man seeks perfection but lives in an imperfect world; complete happiness belongs to Paradise
Yes. Finding joy in small things does not satisfy his nature.
questions.rationale: “Man by nature is a perfectionist, born in an imperfect world. It is this contradiction that creates problems.”

questions.q: Zakat is described as “an annual reminder.” Of what?
options: That everything a person has belongs to God and others have a rightful share in it
Correct. A selfish stance is a wrong stance.
That taxes are due to the state
Not quite. The article says: That everything a person has belongs to God and others have a rightful share in it.
That the year has ended
Not quite. The article says: That everything a person has belongs to God and others have a rightful share in it.
That wealth should be hidden
Not quite. The article says: That everything a person has belongs to God and others have a rightful share in it.
questions.rationale: “Zakat is an annual reminder to man that everything he possesses belongs to God, and that nothing should, therefore, be withheld from Him.”

questions.q: On a very hot day the electricity returned and the fan began to turn. What did this bring to the author’s mind?
options: The discomforts of city life
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s passing from the hardship of this world to the joy of Paradise.
The cleverness of inventors
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s passing from the hardship of this world to the joy of Paradise.
The believer’s passing from the hardship of this world to the joy of Paradise
Well read. A material event became a spiritual one.
The importance of electricity
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s passing from the hardship of this world to the joy of Paradise.
questions.rationale: “The period of worldly suffering will instantly end and the joyous period of Paradise shall begin… The material incident was converted into a spiritual one.”

questions.q: The Arabic word for fasting, sawm, means abstinence. How does the article connect this with a “man of mission”?
options: One devoted to a mission gives up all that distracts from it; fasting is training in that spirit
Yes. Simple living, high thinking.
Missions should last only a month
Not quite. The article says: One devoted to a mission gives up all that distracts from it; fasting is training in that spirit.
Abstinence is the mission itself
Not quite. The article says: One devoted to a mission gives up all that distracts from it; fasting is training in that spirit.
A man of mission never eats in public
Not quite. The article says: One devoted to a mission gives up all that distracts from it; fasting is training in that spirit.
questions.rationale: “When one involves himself in a mission, he abstains from all diversions… Abstaining from food and water for a limited period is symbolic training.”

questions.q: Many people feel their abilities were never appreciated. What two options does the article say they have?
options: To wait, or to move abroad
Not quite. The article says: To work within what others have built, or to create one’s own world by one’s own effort.
To complain, or to remain silent
Not quite. The article says: To work within what others have built, or to create one’s own world by one’s own effort.
To work within what others have built, or to create one’s own world by one’s own effort
Right. There is no third option.
To seek praise, or to give up
Not quite. The article says: To work within what others have built, or to create one’s own world by one’s own effort.
questions.rationale: “One is to accept an establishment made by someone else. The other is to create one’s own world… In this world, no one else can do your work.”

questions.q: What did Job say when he lost everything he had?
options: “Why has this happened to me?”
Not quite. The article says: “The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken; blessed be the name of the Lord”.
“I shall win it all back”
Not quite. The article says: “The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken; blessed be the name of the Lord”.
“The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken; blessed be the name of the Lord”
Yes. He is called the epitome of patience.
“There is no justice”
Not quite. The article says: “The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken; blessed be the name of the Lord”.
questions.rationale: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return… the Lord gave, and Lord hath taken; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

questions.q: Why does the article call death “an undiscovered reality,” though everyone knows of it?
options: Doctors cannot define it
Not quite. The article says: People treat it as news about others and never apply it to themselves.
It happens too rarely to notice
Not quite. The article says: People treat it as news about others and never apply it to themselves.
No one has returned to describe it
Not quite. The article says: People treat it as news about others and never apply it to themselves.
People treat it as news about others and never apply it to themselves
Exactly. They live only in the present.
questions.rationale: “People see or hear of this regularly, but everyone takes it as external news. No one applies it personally.”

questions.q: A scientist is quoted as saying, “We know more and more about less and less.” What point does the article draw from this?
options: Scientists know less than their forebears
Not quite. The article says: Science gives only partial knowledge of reality and cannot by itself reach the ultimate truth.
Science has stopped making progress
Not quite. The article says: Science gives only partial knowledge of reality and cannot by itself reach the ultimate truth.
Specialisation should be banned
Not quite. The article says: Science gives only partial knowledge of reality and cannot by itself reach the ultimate truth.
Science gives only partial knowledge of reality and cannot by itself reach the ultimate truth
Well reasoned. Hence renewed interest in religion.
questions.rationale: “It is now an accepted fact among the scientific community that science gives us but a partial knowledge of reality.”
